name: Cell Theory
statement: All living things are made of cells, the basic unit of life, and every cell comes from a cell.
statementAccent: every cell comes from a cell
meaning: Cell theory is the foundational principle that all living organisms are composed of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, and that all cells arise only from pre-existing cells. It unifies the whole diversity of life at a single level: from bacteria to whales, living things are built of cells, and new cells come not from spontaneous formation but from the division of existing ones.
mechanism: The theory rests on three tenets built up over two centuries of observation. First, organisms are made of cells, so the cell is the common denominator of life. Second, the cell is the smallest unit that carries out the functions of life, from metabolism to reproduction. Third, captured in the phrase every cell from a cell, new cells arise only by the division of existing cells, which rules out spontaneous generation. Later additions note that cells carry hereditary DNA passed on at division, that energy flow occurs within cells, and that all cells share a basic chemistry.

examples.text: Robert Hooke coined the word cell in 1665 for the tiny compartments he saw in cork, though these were the empty walls of dead plant cells, not living ones.
Matthias Schleiden for plants in 1838 and Theodor Schwann for animals in 1839 formulated the classical theory, unifying botany and zoology under the cell.
Rudolf Virchow popularised the third tenet in 1855, that all cells arise from pre-existing cells, rejecting spontaneous generation.

variants.name: The modern additions
variants.text: Extensions holding that cells carry hereditary information passed on during division, that metabolism and energy flow occur within cells, and that all cells share a basic chemical composition.

variants.name: The Virchow-Remak dispute
variants.text: The historical controversy that Robert Remak showed cells arise by division before Virchow, who is often said to have presented the idea without proper credit.

whyItMatters: It is one of the foundational, unifying principles of modern biology, linking every organism at the level of the cell and grounding physiology, genetics, and medicine. By locating life and its continuity in the cell, it framed Virchow's cellular pathology, the idea that disease arises from cellular abnormality, and it remains the bedrock on which the study of living things is built.

working.text: treat the cell as the basic unit of structure and function when analysing any organism, from microbe to mammal.
assume new cells come from the division of existing ones, not from spontaneous formation.
recognise that viruses, being acellular, sit outside the theory, which concerns cellular life.

limits: It is a foundational, well-established theory, but it concerns cellular life and leaves debated edge cases. Viruses are acellular, not made of cells, so they fall outside the theory, and whether they count as living remains disputed. The number of tenets counted as modern cell theory varies between sources. And its history carries genuine controversy, notably the dispute over whether Virchow took the every-cell-from-a-cell principle from Remak without adequate credit.
misreadings: Robert Hooke did not see living cells; he observed the empty walls of dead cork and did not think them alive, and the word cell came from their resemblance to small rooms. Schleiden and Schwann founded the theory but held some mistaken ideas, including that cells could form afresh in a crystallisation-like way, which the every-cell-from-a-cell principle later overturned. And the theory does not settle whether viruses are alive, since they lie outside cellular life.
origin: Built over two centuries: Robert Hooke named the cell in 1665 and Leeuwenhoek observed living microbes in the 1670s; Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann formulated the classical theory in 1838 and 1839, and Rudolf Virchow added that cells arise from cells in 1855.
